content: The relationship between total funding and total blood donations reported across countries reveals significant variations in funding levels per collection among different income groups. Generally, economically developed countries exhibit higher funding per collection. However, even within the same income group, disparities in funding levels are evident. Alarmingly, many lowand lower-middle-income countries report very low funding per collection or heavy reliance on external financial support. In terms of funding sources, countries reported varying combinations of government budget allocations, cost recovery mechanisms, and external donor contributions. For instance, 57% of countries reported having a dedicated government budget line item, while 60% combined government funding with cost recovery. Conversely, 29% relied solely on cost recovery, and 20% had neither government budget allocations nor cost recovery mechanisms in place. The organization of blood collection and processing facilities is critical for efficient resource utilization. National blood services should be coordinated by the Ministry of Health to ensure cost-effectiveness. Blood transfusion services may operate under a single provider, such as a national blood transfusion service, or through multiple organizations. Regardless of the model, coordination at national, regional, and provincial levels is essential, with activities like blood screening and processing ideally consolidated in strategic locations. Globally, 13,282 blood centers were reported in 2013, with 18% being stand-alone centers and 58% hospital-based. The Western Pacific Region had the highest proportion of stand-alone blood centers, and it also processed the highest average number of test samples per blood-screening center or laboratory among all WHO regions. Quality assurance and monitoring are vital for blood safety. A total of 155 countries (87% of reporting countries) reported having national standards for blood collection, testing, processing, storage, and distribution. However, only 55% of countries had systems for regular inspection of blood transfusion services, and 57% had licensing systems for these services. Furthermore, 67% of countries reported having national external quality assessment schemes for laboratory screening of transfusion-transmissible infections, while 52% had similar schemes for blood group serology and compatibility testing. Accreditation of national blood transfusion services remains limited, with only 30% of countries reporting accreditation. Europe leads in this area, with 58% of its countries having accredited services, compared to much lower percentages in other regions. Additionally, 64% of countries reported having continuing education programs for blood transfusion personnel, and 41% offered nationally recognized university degrees or diplomas in blood transfusion medicine or science. The availability of blood and blood products for transfusion varies widely. There are no global standards for estimating national blood requirements, and the need for blood is influenced by factors such as health service coverage and the sophistication of healthcare systems. Low-income countries often face insufficient blood collection to meet their healthcare needs. Strategies to improve blood collection, including promoting regular voluntary non-remunerated blood donation, are essential for ensuring sustainable and safe blood supplies. Donor retention is a critical factor in improving blood safety. Countries with high donor retention rates, such as South Africa, have significantly lower prevalence rates of transfusion-transmissible infections among blood donors compared to the general population. Emphasizing donor retention strategies is crucial for achieving similar safety levels in other regions. Laboratory screening and testing of donor blood are fundamental for blood safety. However, some countries still lack the capacity to test for all markers of transfusion-transmissible infections, compromising the safety of their blood supplies. Inadequate screening coverage, particularly in lowand middle-income countries, poses significant risks. Efforts must focus on improving the quality and coverage of blood screening to ensure safer transfusion practices. The clinical use of blood is another critical aspect of blood safety. Evidence-based transfusion guidelines and audits can reduce unnecessary exposure to allogeneic blood and optimize the use of this scarce resource. However, many countries lack national guidelines or fail to implement them effectively. Hospital transfusion committees can play a pivotal role in promoting judicious blood use and ensuring adherence to guidelines. Data on the clinical use of blood and blood products are often incomplete due to the diversity of institutions performing transfusions and variable documentation practices. The proportion of blood transfused as whole blood versus components varies significantly among countries, reflecting differences in healthcare system development. As health systems advance, component therapy becomes increasingly important for patient management. In summary, while progress has been made in blood collection, quality assurance, and clinical use, significant challenges remain, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Addressing these challenges requires coordinated efforts to improve funding, infrastructure, quality systems, and education, ensuring equitable access to safe and effective blood transfusion services globally.
